body:
When a detached Docker-isolated command dies, `$` preserves everything needed to continue it — the container filesystem, the log, the execution record — but offers no way to actually **get back into it**. The only documented recovery is raw `docker`, and for a stopped container that means re-running the original entrypoint from scratch.

## What happened

A long-running detached session crashed ~28 hours in:

```
$ --status 0ea1c630-cfdf-477e-8528-29d175a7fe64
  status executed
  exitCode 139
  oomKilled false
  isolated docker / isolationMode detached
  sessionName dd1acfbe-3c01-4ffa-8c78-f825457f5813
  containerId a182caf61c25275ef71da31954e7e542e140056c7519d4abd7b0296d077b9b31
```

The container was retained (27 GB writable layer) with the complete working tree still in it. The guidance printed on failure was:

```
Inspect: docker exec -it dd1acfbe-... sh (if running) or docker start -ai dd1acfbe-...
```

`docker exec` is unavailable (the container is stopped), and `docker start -ai` **re-runs the original command from the beginning** — which for a multi-hour AI task means throwing away a day of work and starting over. There is no `$`-level path from a preserved container back to useful work.

## What is missing

**1. Attach to a running detached session's terminal**

There is `--status`, `--stop`, `--terminate`, `--upload-log` — but nothing to watch or interact with a live detached command. Something like:

```
$ --attach <uuid-or-session>          # attach to the container's terminal
$ --attach <id> --read-only           # follow output without stdin
```

Today the only option is tailing `logPath`, which is one-way.

**2. Resume a finished/crashed session in its own container context**

The valuable thing after a crash is the container's **filesystem state** — the checkout, the caches, the intermediate artifacts. Please support re-entering it:

```
$ --resume <uuid-or-session>                    # restart the stored command in the same container
$ --resume <uuid-or-session> -- <new command>   # run a DIFFERENT command in that same context
```

The second form is the one that matters most for downstream users. A supervisor that knows how to continue its own work (e.g. `solve --resume <tool-session-id>`) needs to run *that* command against the crashed container's filesystem, not the original command again. Ideally this keeps the **same execution UUID / session name**, so `--status`, `--list` and `--upload-log` continue to address one logical session across restarts rather than fragmenting into unrelated records.

**3. Resume everything that was running, after a supervisor restart**

If the process that launched the sessions is killed and restarted, it needs a way to pick all of them back up:

```
$ --resume-all          # re-attach/resume every execution still marked running
$ --list --running      # machine-readable set to drive that
```

Right now a restarted supervisor can enumerate records via `--list`, but has no primitive to reconnect or continue them, so in-flight work is silently orphaned. In the incident above the crash was at 14:07Z and was not acted on until 20:14Z, purely because the supervisor had restarted in between.

## Side note: `oomKilled=false` is correct but not enough

The record says `exitCode 139, oomKilled false`, and consumers reasonably read that as "not a memory problem". The run had in fact died of memory exhaustion — a **V8 heap-limit abort** inside the launched Node process:

```
FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
12: v8::internal::Runtime_RegExpExecMultiple(...)
```

`oomKilled` reflects the kernel/cgroup OOM killer, which genuinely did not fire (`cgroup oom_kill=0`, 9.1 GB of 11.7 GB free), so the flag is not wrong — but paired with exit 139 it actively misleads. Since `$` already parses the log footer for the exit code, it could surface a hint when the log contains a fatal memory marker, e.g. an extra `exitReason memory-exhaustion (v8-heap-limit)` field. Related to the earlier work in #144, #148 and #151.

## Why this matters

Everything needed for recovery already survives: the log, the record, the container. The gap is purely the missing verbs. With `--attach`, `--resume [-- <cmd>]` and `--resume-all`, a crashed long-running task becomes continuable instead of restart-from-zero — and a supervisor restart stops orphaning work.

comments.body: Downstream consumer needing these verbs: link-assistant/hive-mind#2189 — the Telegram bot recovers the tool session id from a killed run but has no way to re-enter the preserved container to continue it.

title: Docker isolation: no way to attach to, resume, or re-enter a detached session — and no way to resume all running commands after a supervisor restart
